Interactive charts, tables and apps

Source: vignettes/articles/interactive.Rmd
interactive.Rmd

This page shows how to make a sortable table, a hover chart and a small Shiny app in the PHW style. All the data is made up.

Interactive widgets don’t follow use_phw_ggplot(), which only changes ggplot2 charts and flextables. Call phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_plotly() each time you make one. For interactive maps, see Maps and boundaries.

library(phwstyle)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1)
areas <- paste("Area", LETTERS[1:6])
weekly <- expand.grid(week = 1:12, area = areas[1:3]) |>
  mutate(cases = rpois(n(), 8 + 5 * sin(week / 2) + 3 * as.integer(factor(area))))
areas_tab <- tibble(
  area = areas,
  cases = c(120, 85, 64, 19, 23, 48),
  rate = c(41.2, 22.5, 63.1, 10.4, 25.8, 33.3),
  share = cases / sum(cases),
  completeness = c(97, 91, 78, 99, 66, 88)
)

reactable

phw_reactable() styles a data frame with the navy header, striped rows, highlighting and a compact layout. caption sits above the table, and source and date sit below it.

phw_reactable(areas_tab[c("area", "cases", "rate")], caption = "Cases by area",
              source = "Example data", date = "2025-06-30")
Cases by area
Source: Example data
Data correct as of 2025-06-30

Pass any other argument to reactable::reactable(). Your values replace the PHW defaults.

Column formats

Five helpers make colDef() objects for the columns argument.

  • phw_col_bar() draws a bar behind the number, scaled to the column maximum.
  • phw_col_heat() shades each cell along a sequential palette, and picks black or white text to stay readable.
  • phw_col_rag() colours a value red, amber or green from two breaks and adds a shape (▼, ■ or ▲), so the status does not rely on colour alone.
  • phw_col_number() shows a number with thousands separators and digits decimal places.
  • phw_col_percent() shows a proportion as a percentage.
phw_reactable(
  areas_tab, caption = "Cases by area", source = "Example data",
  columns = list(
    area = reactable::colDef(name = "Area"),
    cases = phw_col_bar(areas_tab, cases, name = "Cases"),
    rate = phw_col_heat(areas_tab, rate, name = "Rate per 100,000"),
    share = phw_col_percent(digits = 0, name = "Share of cases"),
    completeness = phw_col_rag(breaks = c(80, 95), digits = 0, name = "Completeness (%)")
  )
)
Cases by area
Source: Example data

digits on phw_reactable() sets the decimal places for every other non-integer column, and a column you format yourself keeps its format. phw_col_number() is the way to set the places for one column:

phw_reactable(areas_tab[c("area", "cases", "rate")], digits = 0,
              columns = list(rate = phw_col_number(digits = 1, name = "Rate")))

Colours that match your charts

Give group_col the column that holds the groups, and each cell takes the colour the same group has in your charts. key names the colour key, as in Colours and accessibility.

phw_reactable(areas_tab[c("area", "cases")], group_col = area, key = "area")

Summary tables

A summary table from phw_summary_table(), phw_crosstab(), phw_rate_table() or phw_risk_table() keeps its bold variable rows and indented levels. It shows without sorting or paging. See Tables for building one.

cases <- tibble(
  age_group = sample(c("0-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  sex = sample(c("Female", "Male"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  outcome = sample(c("Outcome X", "Outcome Y"), 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2))
)
phw_summary_table(cases, by = outcome,
                  labels = list(age_group = "Age group", sex = "Sex")) |>
  phw_reactable(caption = "Characteristics by outcome", source = "Example data")
Characteristics by outcome
Source: Example data
n (%)

Header style and theme

header picks the header style: "booktabs" (navy text and rules, the default), "navy" (a navy band with white text) or "light" (a light teal band). accent changes the header and rule colour.

phw_reactable_theme() returns the same theme as a reactable::reactableTheme(). Use it when you call reactable::reactable() yourself.

reactable::reactable(areas_tab[c("area", "cases")],
                     theme = phw_reactable_theme(header = "navy", font_size = 16),
                     striped = TRUE)
A reactable table with bars, heat shading and status cells

DT

phw_datatable() gives a searchable, sortable and paged table. It takes caption, source, date and digits like the other renderers. page_length sets the rows per page, and ... goes to DT::datatable().

phw_datatable(weekly, caption = "Cases by week and area", source = "Example data",
              page_length = 6, filter = "top")
Cases by week and area
Source: Example data

Use options for DataTables options, such as options = list(dom = "t") to show only the table.

plotly

phw_plotly() styles a plotly chart: PHW colours, the Ubuntu font, a legend under the chart, and the source line. It takes a ggplot or a plotly object. legend is "bottom", "right" or "none". modebar = FALSE hides the tool bar.

From a ggplot 

g <- ggplot(weekly, aes(week, cases, colour = area)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Cases")
phw_plotly(g, source = "Example data", hovermode = "x")

Extra arguments go to plotly::layout(), so hovermode = "x" above shows all areas for one week at once. Lists are merged with the PHW defaults, so title = list(text = "Cases by week") keeps the PHW title style.

From plot_ly() 

p <- plotly::plot_ly(weekly, x = ~week, y = ~cases, color = ~area,
                     type = "scatter", mode = "lines")
phw_plotly(p, source = "Example data", legend = "right")

Colour keys and colour scales

A plotly chart takes its colours from the palette argument unless a trace sets its own. For colours that stay with a group across charts, pass the colour key to plotly:

keyed <- plotly::plot_ly(weekly, x = ~week, y = ~cases, color = ~area,
                         colors = phw_colour_key(weekly$area, "area"),
                         type = "scatter", mode = "lines")
phw_plotly(keyed, source = "Example data")

A ggplot keeps the colours of its scale_colour_phw_d(key = ).

phw_plotly_colorscale() turns a PHW palette into a plotly colour scale, for heatmaps and markers coloured by a number. reverse = TRUE flips it and n sets the steps.

heat <- plotly::plot_ly(z = volcano, type = "heatmap",
                        colorscale = phw_plotly_colorscale("teals"))
phw_plotly(heat, source = "Example data")
A plotly line chart in the PHW style

Shiny and bslib

phw_page_navbar() builds a complete app page with the PHW header band, a navy navigation bar and a footer. It takes nav_panel() tabs like bslib::page_navbar(). title and subtitle fill the header, and footer = FALSE drops the footer.

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
use_phw_ggplot()

ui <- phw_page_navbar(
  title = "Weekly surveillance",
  subtitle = "Team name",
  nav_panel("Overview", card(card_header("Cases by week"), plotOutput("trend"))),
  nav_panel("Data", reactable::reactableOutput("table"))
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$trend <- renderPlot(
    ggplot(weekly, aes(week, cases, colour = area)) + geom_line() +
      scale_colour_phw_d(key = "area")
  )
  output$table <- reactable::renderReactable(phw_reactable(areas_tab))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

phw_bs_theme() is the theme behind the page. Use it on any bslib or Shiny page, and add your own values. They override the PHW ones.

theme <- phw_bs_theme(primary = "#24A2B5")
phw_page_navbar(title = "Weekly surveillance", theme = theme)

phw_page_navbar(theme = ) takes it, and so do bslib::page() and fluidPage(theme = ) in an app of your own.

phw_header() makes only the header band, for a page that doesn’t use phw_page_navbar(). With logo = FALSE, or when the logo isn’t installed, it shows the organisation name instead. See Installation and setup.

phw_header(title = "Weekly surveillance", subtitle = "Team name", logo = FALSE)

A working app comes with the package. Run it, and copy it as a starting point:

shiny::runApp(system.file("examples", "shiny", package = "phwstyle"))
The example Shiny app with a sidebar, value boxes, a chart and a table

The gallery shows more interactive outputs.
